title: Drive Motors & Drivetrain Sizing
scope_note: Drive motors, gearboxes, wheels, hubs, and drivetrain sizing for 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight combat robots, covering FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, N-series, Pololu, and brushless options plus the physics formulas used to size a drivetrain.

entities.name: FingerTech "Silver Spark" 16mm Gearmotor, 33.3:1
entities.summary: 33.3:1 Silver Spark antweight gearmotor: a 16 mm all-metal spur gearbox mated to a Mabuchi FK-050 motor with a 3 mm D shaft.
pros: All-metal gearbox is far more durable than plastic-geared alternatives
9 stock ratios cover the whole speed/torque range antweights need
Extra-long 3mm shaft allows direct (live-axle) wheel mounting
Very well documented, huge installed base, easy to source spares
cons: More expensive per unit than generic N20/N30 motors
Bare motor (not brushless) has lower efficiency and shorter brush life than premium brushless drive pods
600:1 and 300:1 ratios are fragile-ish under sustained stall loads
entities.notes: The old record incorrectly used the raw motor's 11,530 rpm as the geared output speed. FingerTech/Palm Beach Bots list about 350 rpm on 2S and 524 rpm on 3S for the 33.3:1 gearbox. 3S operation reduces motor life.

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 11.1:1
entities.summary: The fastest stock Silver Spark ratio, used when a builder wants maximum top speed and dodge/reposition ability rather than pushing torque, typically paired with a larger (~2in) wheel.
pros: Highest stock top speed of the Silver Spark family
Good choice for spinners that just need to aim/dodge, not ram hard
cons: Lowest stock torque of the ladder — can be traction-limited or torque-limited depending on wheel size and weight distribution
entities.notes: Output-speed figures are FingerTech/Palm Beach Bots values at 2S and 3S. The underlying FK-050 motor is nominally 6 V; running higher voltage increases speed and reduces motor life.

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 100:1
entities.summary: A mid-high torque Silver Spark ratio popular on control bots and lifters that need strong pushing/lifting force more than raw speed.
pros: High torque headroom, good for pushing/wedge bots and small lifter actuation
Same footprint/price as every other Silver Spark ratio
cons: Slow top speed, not ideal for a bot that needs to dodge quickly
entities.notes: Output-speed figures are FingerTech/Palm Beach Bots values at 2S and 3S. The underlying FK-050 motor is nominally 6 V; running higher voltage increases speed and reduces motor life.

entities.name: FingerTech Silver Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 200:1
entities.summary: One of the highest stock-ratio Silver Sparks, used for slow, high-torque applications like weapon lifters, self-righters, or extremely traction-limited pushing bots rather than main drive.
pros: Very high torque for its size/weight
Same base motor reliability as the rest of the line
cons: Far too slow for main drive on a competitive bot
At this ratio the output gear stage becomes the limiting strength factor, not the motor
entities.notes: Output-speed figures are FingerTech/Palm Beach Bots values at 2S and 3S. The underlying FK-050 motor is nominally 6 V; running higher voltage increases speed and reduces motor life.

entities.name: FingerTech "Gold Spark" 16mm Gearmotor
entities.summary: FingerTech's budget-tier 16mm gearmotor: the same Mabuchi FK-050 base motor as the Silver Spark but with a plastic (not all-metal) gear stage, sold in 8 ratios from 20:1 to 360:1. Positioned for hobby/mini-sumo/line-following use and lighter-duty antweight builds rather than front-line competitive drive.
pros: Cheaper than Silver Spark for the same base motor
Fine for plastic antweights and lighter-contact builds
Same 11mm face-mount pattern as Silver Spark for easy swapping
cons: Plastic final gear stage is explicitly rated to fail above 6.84 kg-cm (95 oz-in) output torque
Not recommended as the sole drive on a bot expected to take direct hits or heavy ramming loads
entities.notes: Ratio ladder: 20:1, 35:1, 50:1, 86:1, 115:1, 150:1, 250:1, 360:1. All ratios share the same 28g weight and $14.79 price point per FingerTech's page. Output rpm/torque here computed from the shared base motor (11,530 RPM / 0.0461 kg-cm) at an assumed ~0.65 efficiency (lower than Silver Spark due to the plastic stage) — medium confidence.

entities.name: FingerTech Gold Spark 16mm Gearmotor, 150:1
entities.summary: A higher-torque Gold Spark ratio near the top of its safe operating range before hitting the plastic output gear's 6.84 kg-cm damage threshold.
pros: Cheap way to get real torque for a plastic-ant lifter or pusher
cons: Approaching the gearbox's rated damage threshold under stall; avoid pinning at full stall for long periods
entities.notes: Estimated output figures at ~0.65 efficiency; medium/low confidence on exact torque number.

entities.name: FingerTech Brushless Mega Spark 1500KV Planetary Gearmotor
entities.summary: 24mm brushless planetary drive gearmotor using FingerTech's FT1806 1500KV motor and a 27:1 all-metal planetary gearbox.
pros: All-metal planetary gearbox is far more torque-dense and durable than a spur gearbox
Brushless motor avoids brush wear
cons: Oversized/heavy for a standard 1 lb antweight budget; more common on beetleweights
Requires a reversing brushless ESC, adding cost/weight/complexity vs a plug-and-play brushed motor
entities.notes: Current post-Sept-2025 version uses M3 face-mount screws on a 19mm circle and is assembled with threadlocker. The long 6mm output shaft contributes materially to the listed 71.5g weight.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini Brushed" Mk2 Antweight Gearmotor
entities.summary: Antweight brushed planetary gearmotor using a custom 030 motor and 16 mm, 22.6:1 all-metal gearbox, available with 3 or 4 mm D shafts.
pros: Planetary gearbox is more durable under shock loading than a single-stage spur gearbox
Popular, well-regarded in the antweight community as a Silver Spark alternative
cons: Costs more than a Silver Spark or generic N20
Exact published RPM/torque/current spec table was not accessible in this research pass
entities.notes: Manufacturer recommends 3S. The 3 mm shaft version is 26.5 g; the 4 mm shaft version is 27.5 g. Face-mount screw engagement is limited to about 2 mm.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini" Brushless 1106 Mk4.1 Gearmotor
entities.summary: 1106 3500KV brushless antweight gearmotor with a 16 mm all-metal planetary gearbox in 28.5:1 drive or 107:1 high-reduction versions.
pros: Brushless motor = no brush wear, higher efficiency, higher power density than a same-size brushed motor
Metal planetary gearbox handles shock loads better than spur gears
Rated for 2S-4S, so voltage alone can retune top speed without swapping hardware
cons: Requires a reversing brushless ESC (not a simple brushed H-bridge)
Sensorless brushless motors can cog/stutter at very low duty cycle / near-stall, an issue brushed motors don't have
Historically has had periods of being sold out due to demand
entities.notes: 28.5:1 drive version: 22.4 g with 3 mm shaft or 23.2 g with 4 mm shaft. 107:1 high-reduction version: 27.3 g / 28.3 g and about 31 mm body length.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics "Mini Pro" 1106 Gearmotor
entities.summary: A higher-spec / higher-price variant of Repeat's 1106 brushless antweight drive gearmotor line, sold alongside the standard Mk4.1 for builders wanting extra performance or refinement (e.g. better bearings, tighter tolerances).
pros: Positioned as the premium option in Repeat's antweight brushless lineup
cons: More than double the price of the standard Mini Brushless variant
Detailed spec differences vs the standard Mk4.1 were not confirmed in this pass
entities.notes: Price ($42) confirmed from the Repeat Robotics shop listing; exact technical differentiation from the standard Mini Brushless 1106 was not available in the pages fetched.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Compact Brushless 1806 Planetary Gearmotor
entities.summary: Integrated 1806-2300KV brushless motor and 22.6:1 planetary gearbox with a hardened 4mm output shaft.
pros: Very light for a brushless beetleweight motor
Hardened steel 4mm shaft with dual bearings on the gearbox output
cons: Sized and priced for 3 lb beetleweight, oversized/overpriced for a standard 1 lb antweight budget
entities.notes: Repeat lists a 20A-or-larger ESC recommendation. The replacement motor alone is listed at 22.4g. Product is currently shown as sold out, but the specifications remain useful for existing robots.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: Reference entry for the Generic N20 Gearmotor form factor/gear-ratio class. Generic marketplace N-series gearmotors are not standardized enough for one exact electrical or torque specification.
pros: Extremely cheap (a few dollars each), widely available from many sellers
Small and light, good for plastic antweights on a tight budget
cons: Quality varies drastically unit to unit and listing to listing (the "quality lottery")
Many units mix plastic gears into otherwise "metal gear" listings
No standardized spec sheet across sellers — published numbers are unreliable
entities.notes: Marketplace N-series gearmotors that share the same outside dimensions and advertised ratio can use different windings, gear materials, shaft lengths, no-load speeds, stall currents, and torque. Use a specific manufacturer/model record for calculations; current FingerTech N10/N20 Spark entries are included elsewhere in the database as verified examples.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 6V, 298:1
entities.summary: Reference entry for the Generic N20 Gearmotor form factor/gear-ratio class. Generic marketplace N-series gearmotors are not standardized enough for one exact electrical or torque specification.
pros: High torque per dollar
Directly confirmed real-world sale listing (298:1, 50 RPM, 6V) validates the ~15,000 RPM bare-motor assumption
cons: Same quality-lottery risk as all generic N-series motors
Too slow alone for a competitive main-drive ratio
entities.notes: Marketplace N-series gearmotors that share the same outside dimensions and advertised ratio can use different windings, gear materials, shaft lengths, no-load speeds, stall currents, and torque. Use a specific manufacturer/model record for calculations; current FingerTech N10/N20 Spark entries are included elsewhere in the database as verified examples.

entities.name: Generic N20 Gearmotor, 12V, 1000:1
entities.summary: Reference entry for the Generic N20 Gearmotor form factor/gear-ratio class. Generic marketplace N-series gearmotors are not standardized enough for one exact electrical or torque specification.
pros: Reinforced gearbox stage rated to ~25 kg*mm (2.5 kg-cm), higher than the ~20 kg*mm (2.0 kg-cm) rating of lower ratios
Very high torque for actuators/lifters
cons: Far too slow for drive; this ratio belongs on weapon-lift or self-righting mechanisms, not wheels
Gearbox is 3.5mm longer than other ratios, a minor packaging difference
entities.notes: Marketplace N-series gearmotors that share the same outside dimensions and advertised ratio can use different windings, gear materials, shaft lengths, no-load speeds, stall currents, and torque. Use a specific manufacturer/model record for calculations; current FingerTech N10/N20 Spark entries are included elsewhere in the database as verified examples.

entities.name: Generic N30 Gearmotor, 6V, 50:1
entities.summary: Reference entry for the Generic N30 Gearmotor form factor/gear-ratio class. Generic marketplace N-series gearmotors are not standardized enough for one exact electrical or torque specification.
pros: More torque and current headroom than N20 for a modest weight increase
Still cheap relative to name-brand combat motors
cons: Same quality-lottery sourcing risk as other generic N-series motors
Larger diameter can be harder to package in a slim 1 lb chassis than a 16mm motor
entities.notes: Marketplace N-series gearmotors that share the same outside dimensions and advertised ratio can use different windings, gear materials, shaft lengths, no-load speeds, stall currents, and torque. Use a specific manufacturer/model record for calculations; current FingerTech N10/N20 Spark entries are included elsewhere in the database as verified examples.

entities.name: Generic N10 Gearmotor, 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: Reference entry for the Generic N10 Gearmotor form factor/gear-ratio class. Generic marketplace N-series gearmotors are not standardized enough for one exact electrical or torque specification.
pros: Lightest option in the N-series family
Cheap and small enough for micro-scale plastic antweights
cons: Least torque and current handling of the family
Least standardized specs / hardest to verify quality before buying
entities.notes: Marketplace N-series gearmotors that share the same outside dimensions and advertised ratio can use different windings, gear materials, shaft lengths, no-load speeds, stall currents, and torque. Use a specific manufacturer/model record for calculations; current FingerTech N10/N20 Spark entries are included elsewhere in the database as verified examples.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor HP 6V, 30:1
entities.summary: Pololu's High-Power (HP) tune of its popular micro metal gearmotor line at a fast 30:1 ratio: a 10x12mm all-metal gearbox on a 3mm D-shaft output, favoring speed and current draw over the LP/MP tunes of the same physical motor.
pros: Precision-manufactured, far more consistent unit-to-unit than generic N-series motors
Well documented performance curves from Pololu
Very compact 10x12mm gearbox cross-section
cons: More expensive than generic N20 motors
3mm output shaft is short (9mm) — needs a hub or coupler, not usually long enough for direct antweight wheel mounting like a Silver Spark
entities.notes: HP variant free-run current is ~100mA and stall current ~1.6A at 6V (confirmed). Exact no-load RPM at 30:1 was not independently confirmed this pass; Pololu's published family typically gives high-hundreds to low-thousands RPM at this ratio (medium/low confidence on the exact figure — verify against the specific product's datasheet before final BOM lock).

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor MP 6V, 30:1
entities.summary: The Medium-Power (MP) tune of Pololu's micro metal gearmotor, splitting the difference between the low-current LP and high-current HP versions of the same physical gearbox and ratio.
pros: Lower current draw than HP for the same ratio, easing ESC/battery sizing
Same precision metal gearbox as HP/LP
cons: Less torque/power than the HP tune at the same ratio
entities.notes: Stall current (0.67A) and free-run current (~70mA) at 6V are confirmed from Pololu's published data; RPM/torque at this specific ratio were not independently confirmed this pass.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor LP 6V, 50:1
entities.summary: The Low-Power (LP) tune of Pololu's micro metal gearmotor, drawing the least current of the three power tunes for a given ratio — useful when a builder is current-budget constrained (e.g. a very small ESC or shared receiver battery).
pros: Lowest current draw of the family, easiest on small ESCs
Same durable metal gearbox as MP/HP
cons: Least torque/power of the three tunes — can be traction- and power-limited on a heavier antweight
entities.notes: Stall current (0.36A) and free-run current (~40mA) at 6V confirmed from Pololu data.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor HP 6V, 100:1
entities.summary: A commonly chosen ratio/power combination for antweight-scale robots wanting a precision-made alternative to generic N20 motors, balancing speed and torque for typical 1.5-2in wheels.
pros: Good balance of speed and torque for a typical 1.5-2in antweight wheel
Precision metal gearbox, consistent unit to unit
Compact 10x12mm gearbox
cons: Higher stall current draw than MP/LP tunes — size ESC accordingly
Short 9mm output shaft needs a hub/coupler
entities.notes: Stall current confirmed from the HP family spec (1.6A at 6V); exact no-load RPM/torque at 100:1 specifically was not independently re-confirmed this pass — Pololu's own product page datasheet should be checked for the final number before locking a BOM.

entities.name: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotor, Extended Motor Shaft variant
entities.summary: A version of the micro metal gearmotor line with the motor's rear shaft extended through the back of the case, letting a builder mount an encoder disc, a second small pulley, or a cooling/inertia element on the motor's non-gearbox end without modifying the motor.
pros: Enables encoder feedback or a rear-mounted pulley/sprocket without custom machining
Same gearbox performance as the standard version
cons: Small weight/cost premium over the standard (non-extended) version
Rarely needed on a simple 2WD antweight without closed-loop control
entities.notes: Useful mainly for control-bot builders who want wheel-speed encoders for closed-loop drive, or who need to power a secondary belt/pulley off the back of the motor in a 4WD belt-driven layout.

entities.name: 1104-size Brushless Motor (FPV-derived) for Custom Drive Pods
entities.summary: FPV-derived brushless motor size-class reference for custom drive-pod experimentation, not a standardized purchasable motor.
pros: Very high power-to-weight ratio compared to a brushed motor of similar size
No brushes to wear out
Wide range of kv (winding) options available from FPV motor market
cons: Sensorless variants can cog or stutter at very low speed/duty cycle, hurting fine driving control
Requires a reversing brushless ESC rather than a simple brushed driver
Needs to be built into or bought as part of a gearbox — not a drop-in drive-and-wheel solution by itself
entities.notes: The four-digit FPV size code describes stator geometry, not KV, voltage, shaft, bearings, weight, current rating, or overall can dimensions. Choose and record a specific motor model before drivetrain calculations.

entities.name: 1404-size Brushless Motor (FPV-derived) for Custom Drive Pods
entities.summary: FPV-derived brushless motor size-class reference for custom drive-pod experimentation, not a standardized purchasable motor.
pros: More stator volume than 1104/1106 for a given height, so more torque/current capability
Same FPV-market kv/winding flexibility
cons: Larger diameter can be harder to fit inside a slim antweight chassis
Same brushless-drive complexity: reversing ESC required, sensorless cogging risk at low speed
entities.notes: The four-digit FPV size code describes stator geometry, not KV, voltage, shaft, bearings, weight, current rating, or overall can dimensions. Choose and record a specific motor model before drivetrain calculations.

entities.name: Modified Continuous-Rotation 9g Micro Servo (Drive)
entities.summary: A standard 9g hobby micro servo (e.g. SG90-class) with its position-limiting potentiometer removed or bypassed (replaced with a fixed voltage divider) so it spins continuously instead of to a commanded angle, letting the transmitter's stick position set speed and direction directly with zero external electronics.
pros: No separate ESC/driver needed — plugs straight into a receiver channel
Extremely cheap and small, ideal for gram-constrained plastic antweights
Simple to source and modify with widely available tutorials
cons: Low top speed and low torque compared to a dedicated gearmotor + ESC of similar weight
Modification quality varies (pot removal/centering must be done carefully or the "stopped" position drifts)
Internal gearbox (plastic in cheap servos) is not built for combat shock loads
entities.notes: The standard mod: remove the servo's positional potentiometer and replace it with two fixed resistors (dividing voltage to sit at the servo's centered/neutral setpoint), and often trim/cut a mechanical stop tab inside the gearbox so the output gear can rotate freely. A 1ms pulse spins one direction, 2ms the other, ~1.5ms stops it, mirroring standard RC PWM servo signal ranges.

entities.name: Stock Continuous-Rotation Micro Servo (FS90R-class)
entities.summary: A factory-built continuous-rotation micro servo (no user modification needed), functionally equivalent to a hand-modified 9g servo but sold ready to use, popular for beginner plastic antweight and fairyweight drive.
pros: Zero-modification, works out of the box
Same weight/cost/simplicity benefits as the hand-modified version, with more consistent "stopped" centering
cons: Same low speed/torque ceiling as any 9g-servo-based drive
Still uses a small plastic internal gearbox not designed for combat impacts
entities.notes: A good first-build option for absolute beginners or very light plastic antweights where simplicity and low part count outweigh top-end performance.

entities.name: 16mm Planetary Gearbox Module (generic/Repeat-style)
entities.summary: A multi-stage (typically 2-3 stage) all-metal planetary gearbox module in the same 16mm form factor popularized by FingerTech's spur-gear Spark line, used by Repeat Robotics and others to mate to brushed or brushless motors for higher torque density and durability than a comparable spur gearbox.
pros: Higher mechanical efficiency (typically ~80-90%) than a comparable spur gearbox (~65-80%)
Planetary gear meshing distributes load across multiple planet gears, more shock-tolerant than a single spur gear train
More torque-dense for the same envelope size
cons: More expensive and complex to manufacture than a simple spur gearbox
Harder to hand-repair/re-lubricate in the field than an open spur gearbox
entities.notes: Represents the general category of planetary gearboxes used in Repeat Robotics' brushed and brushless antweight drive motors; efficiency figures are typical-range estimates from general gearbox engineering knowledge, not a specific manufacturer's published test data.

entities.name: N-Series (N10/N20/N30) Gearbox: Metal vs Plastic Gear Stages
aliases: N20 metal gear vs plastic gear
entities.summary: A comparison entity describing the inconsistent internal construction of budget N-series gearmotors: many listings advertise "metal gear" but only some internal stages are actually metal, with the rest plastic, and quality varies not just by listing but by individual unit within the same order — the core of the antweight community's "quality lottery" problem with these motors.
pros: When a unit is good, it is very cheap for the torque delivered
All-metal-gear versions do exist and can be nearly as durable as name-brand options at a fraction of the cost
cons: No reliable way to verify actual gear material from a listing photo or description alone
Reported failure modes include stripped final-stage gears, inconsistent KV/no-load speed between "identical" units, and out-of-box dead units
No standardized manufacturer datasheet across the many resellers of what is often the same underlying OEM part
entities.notes: Community-standard mitigation: buy several spares from the start (treat them as a consumable), bench-test every motor before installing it (measure free-run current and no-load RPM, compare across the batch, and reject outliers), and avoid using an untested cheap N-series motor as the sole drive on a bot going into an important match. Name-brand options (FingerTech Silver/Gold Spark, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) cost more specifically because they remove this variance.

entities.name: FingerTech Lite Flite Foam Wheel
entities.summary: FingerTech's neoprene foam wheel, the most widely used antweight wheel: extremely light, shock-absorbing, and surprisingly grippy for a plain foam tire, sold in a wide range of diameters and two widths to fit the Twist/Snap/Lite hub system.
pros: Very light — a major reason it's the default antweight wheel choice
Neoprene foam absorbs shock from arena floor impacts and hazards, protecting the gearbox/shaft
Surprisingly good grip for its weight, especially versus hard plastic wheels
Wide diameter range (25.4-76.2mm / 1.0-3.0in in 6.35mm/0.25in steps) lets builders dial in speed vs torque without changing motors
cons: Less absolute grip than a silicone-coated or compliant rubber tread wheel
Foam compresses/wears over many hard hits, eventually needs replacement
Needs a separate hub (Lite/Snap/Twist) adding a small amount of weight and an assembly step
entities.notes: A 2.00in diameter tire alone weighs about 0.14oz (~4g); smaller/larger diameters scale roughly with tire volume. Widths available: 12.7mm (0.5in, "Thin") and 19.1mm (0.75in, "Wide"). Plastic hubs used with Lite Flites weigh about 3g each, so a full wheel+hub assembly at 1.5-2in is roughly 7-10g depending on width and hub choice.

entities.name: Silicone-Coated / Cast Silicone Tire
entities.summary: A foam or 3D-printed wheel core coated or wrapped in a thin layer of cast silicone rubber (Shore A ~20-50 durometer), a common DIY upgrade path when bare foam or bare plastic doesn't provide enough grip for a control bot or pushing match.
pros: Significant traction improvement over bare foam or bare plastic/TPU
Durometer is tunable by the builder (softer = more grip but faster wear, harder = more durable but less grip)
Can be applied over an existing lightweight foam or printed core, keeping most of the weight savings
cons: Requires casting/mixing 2-part silicone rubber (extra build step, cure time, some skill)
Adds some weight over bare foam
Tackier compounds pick up arena debris faster, sometimes needing cleaning mid-event
entities.notes: Shore A 30-50 durometer silicone/urethane compounds are commonly cited as delivering the best grip on polished wood or acrylic arena floors without being so soft they wear out quickly or gum up with debris.

entities.name: 3D-Printed TPU Wheel
entities.summary: A wheel (tire, or tire+hub as one piece) 3D printed in flexible TPU filament (commonly 85-95A shore hardness), a zero-marginal-cost option extremely popular in plastic antweights since it fits the class's plastic-construction ethos and needs no purchased hub/tire hardware.
pros: Essentially free if you already own a printer and filament
Can be printed as a single piece with the hub/shaft-bore built in, saving assembly and weight of a separate metal hub
Tread pattern, diameter, and width are all fully custom per design
Very impact-resistant, harder to crack than rigid printed wheels
cons: TPU can be harder to print reliably (stringing, needs a direct-drive extruder ideally) than rigid filaments
Grip is generally lower than a soft cast-silicone tire at similar hardness, though still much better than a rigid PLA/PETG wheel
Print layer lines/infill can affect roundness/balance if not printed carefully
entities.notes: Common shore hardness for printable TPU filament is 85A-95A; softer (lower shore) TPUs exist but are harder to print and more prone to tearing on impact.

entities.name: O-Ring Tire Wheel
entities.summary: A lightweight wheel technique where a plain hub (aluminum, printed plastic, or Delrin) has a groove sized to hold a rubber O-ring (or several stacked), which is stretched onto the hub's outer diameter to act as a cheap, easily replaceable, grippy tire.
pros: Very cheap and easy to replace when worn or damaged — just pull off the old o-ring and stretch on a new one
Rubber compound gives solid grip, often better than bare foam
Hub itself can be very light and simple to make or print
cons: O-ring can roll or shift in its groove under high torque/lateral load if the groove isn't sized tightly enough
Less shock absorption than a full foam tire
Buna-N/silicone o-ring compound and durometer choice affects grip and wear, requiring some trial and error
entities.notes: A well-known low-cost DIY approach used across weight classes, including small o-ring sizes on antweight-scale hubs.

entities.name: Banebots T61 Compliant Wheel
entities.summary: A compliant (flexible tread) wheel line from Banebots that conforms to surfaces for extra grip and control, sold in 6 hardness options, 4 diameters, and 4 hub-shaft sizes, primarily sized for beetleweight/hobbyweight but with small diameters usable in heavier antweight or control-bot-focused builds; the smaller Banebots T40 line is aimed more directly at ant/fairy scale.
pros: Compliant rubber tread conforms to the arena floor for better grip and control than a rigid wheel
Wide range of hardness options (10A soft/max-grip up to 60A firm/durable) to tune grip vs longevity
Well-known, widely trusted brand in combat robotics with a long track record
cons: Heavier than a foam or TPU wheel of similar diameter — a real cost on a 1 lb weight budget
Smallest available diameters may still be larger/heavier than what a competitive lightweight antweight wants
entities.notes: T61 compliant hardness options: 10A (yellow, maximum flexibility/grip) and 60A (black, firmer/more durable) were specifically confirmed; the line is stated to offer 6 hardness options total, 4 diameters, and 4 hub shaft sizes. The smaller T40 line is described as better suited to antweight/fairyweight builds.

entities.name: FingerTech Lite Hub
entities.summary: FingerTech's lightest wheel hub, designed to mount common foam wheels onto a 3mm motor shaft with minimal added weight.
pros: Lightest hub option in the FingerTech lineup
Simple, proven, widely used with Lite Flite wheels
cons: Less robust than Snap/Twist hubs under very high shock/torque loads
entities.notes: Approximate weight ~3g each based on general FingerTech plastic-hub weight figures cited for Lite Flite assemblies.

entities.name: FingerTech Snap Hub
entities.summary: An anodized 6061 aluminum hub from FingerTech that holds a foam tire tightly via a custom washer with a recess to prevent the retaining snap ring from coming loose, offering more strength than the plastic Lite Hub at a modest weight cost.
pros: Anodized 6061 aluminum construction is stronger and more durable than plastic hubs
Positive snap-ring retention keeps the tire from working loose over a match
cons: Heavier than the plastic Lite Hub
entities.notes: Exact per-unit weight not confirmed this pass.

entities.name: FingerTech Twist Hub
entities.summary: An anodized 6061 aluminum hub secured to the motor shaft with an 8-32 setscrew, holding the foam tire tightly via a locking washer; sold in Thin (0.50in) and Wide (0.75in) widths for both 3mm and 4mm shafts.
pros: Setscrew retention onto the motor shaft is very secure against slipping under torque
Aluminum build is strong and light
Available for both 3mm and 4mm shafts, and Thin/Wide widths
cons: Heavier than the plastic Lite Hub
Setscrew must be properly torqued/thread-locked or it can back out over repeated hits
entities.notes: Thin (0.50in wide) version confirmed at 5.5g each.

entities.name: GT2 Belt & Pulley Drivetrain Set (antweight scale)
entities.summary: A small GT2 (2mm pitch) timing belt and matching aluminum or 3D-printed pulley set used to link a front and rear wheel on each side of a 4WD antweight, letting two motors drive four wheels instead of needing four separate drive motors.
pros: Gives 4-wheel traction and redundancy (surviving a lifted/high-centered wheel) using only 2 drive motors
GT2 belts are cheap, widely available (from 3D printer supply chains), and don't require the precision of chain
Printed pulleys keep the added weight low
cons: Adds mechanical complexity and a few extra failure points (belt tension, pulley wear, belt skipping teeth under shock)
Extra weight vs a simple 2WD direct-drive layout, competing with armor/weapon weight budget
Belt can be damaged by direct weapon hits if not shielded
entities.notes: A common way to get 4WD traction and pushing power on a 1 lb control bot without the weight and complexity of 4 separate gearmotors and ESCs.

entities.name: Robot Speed from Motor RPM and Wheel Diameter
entities.summary: Converts a drivetrain's output (wheel) RPM and wheel diameter into a theoretical no-load top speed, the first step in sizing any antweight drivetrain.

variables.motor_rpm_no_load: no-load RPM of the bare motor at the chosen nominal voltage
variables.gear_ratio: total gearbox reduction, expressed as N:1 (use N)
variables.v_mph: theoretical no-load top speed in miles per hour (real-world loaded speed is lower)

entities.worked_example: FingerTech Silver Spark at 11.1:1 (motor_rpm_no_load = 11,530 at 7.4V) with a 2.0in wheel: wheel RPM = 11,530 / 11.1 = 1,038.7 RPM. v_mph = 1,038.7 x pi x 2.0 / 1056 = 1,038.7 x 6.283 / 1056 ~= 6.18 mph. This matches commonly reported antweight sprint speeds of roughly 6 mph. Real-world speed under load (current draw sagging the battery voltage, rolling resistance, and wheel slip) typically comes in at ~70-90% of this theoretical number.

entities.name: Required Motor Torque for a Target Acceleration / Pushing Force
entities.summary: Sizes the motor-shaft stall torque needed to accelerate a given robot mass at a target rate (or to sustain a target pushing force), working back through the wheel radius, gear ratio, and gearbox efficiency.
entities.expression: F = m * a;  T_wheel = F * r / n_driven_wheels;  T_motor_stall_required = T_wheel / (gear_ratio * efficiency)

variables.a: target acceleration or deceleration, m/s^2 (e.g. 1-2g for a fast start/ram)
variables.n_driven_wheels: number of powered wheels sharing the load
variables.T_wheel: required torque at the wheel/output shaft, N*m
variables.efficiency: gearbox mechanical efficiency, ~0.65-0.80 for spur gearboxes, ~0.80-0.92 for planetary
variables.T_motor_stall_required: minimum motor-shaft stall torque needed, N*m (convert to kg-cm by dividing N*m by 0.09807)

entities.worked_example: 1 lb robot (m = 0.4536 kg) targeting 2g acceleration (a = 19.6 m/s^2) on two driven wheels of radius 0.019 m (1.5in diameter): F = 0.4536 x 19.6 = 8.89 N. T_wheel per side = 8.89 x 0.019 / 2 = 0.0844 N*m = 0.86 kg-cm. With a 33.3:1 Silver Spark gearbox at ~0.75 efficiency: T_motor_stall_required = 0.86 / (33.3 x 0.75) = 0.0345 kg-cm, comfortably under the Silver Spark's ~0.046 kg-cm bare-motor stall torque, so this ratio has margin to spare for a 2g start. At the fast 11.1:1 ratio, the same math needs 0.86 / (11.1 x 0.75) = 0.103 kg-cm at the motor shaft — more than the bare motor's stall torque can supply, meaning 11.1:1 alone cannot sustain a full 2g acceleration at stall (though brief transient acceleration before the motor reaches that speed is a separate, more forgiving calculation).

entities.name: Traction Limit: Why Torque Beyond Available Grip Is Wasted
entities.summary: Defines the maximum pushing/accelerating force a drivetrain can actually put to the ground, set by wheel-to-floor friction rather than motor torque; any drivetrain torque capacity beyond this ceiling just spins the wheels and wastes battery/heat instead of producing more force.

variables.mu: coefficient of friction between the wheel tread and the arena floor (dimensionless; roughly 0.3-0.5 for bare foam on polycarbonate, 0.5-0.8 for silicone/compliant rubber tread on polycarbonate or wood)
variables.N: normal force pressing the driven wheels into the floor, Newtons (approximately the full robot weight for a 2WD antweight with no significant weight on non-driven casters/skids)
variables.F_max: maximum pushing/traction force before the wheels slip, Newtons

entities.worked_example: 1 lb robot (weight = 0.4536 kg x 9.81 = 4.45 N) on silicone-tread wheels with mu ~= 0.6 on a polycarbonate floor: F_max = 0.6 x 4.45 = 2.67 N. Compare this to the pushing force available at the wheel from formula-required-torque-acceleration-pushing: even the lowest-torque stock Silver Spark ratio (11.1:1, ~0.38 kg-cm output stall torque, ~0.0373 N*m) on a 0.019 m wheel radius over 2 driven wheels can produce up to 2 x 0.0373 / 0.019 = 3.9 N of force at the wheel before the motor itself stalls — already above the 2.67 N traction ceiling. In other words, the wheels slip before the motor runs out of torque, so choosing a slower/higher-torque ratio than 11.1:1 purely to 'push harder' would not actually increase the robot's real-world pushing force; it would only reduce top speed. Common guidance (e.g. from Just 'Cuz Robotics) is to size the gear ratio with roughly 1.5-2x the torque strictly required to reach the traction limit, then optimize the remaining ratio choice for speed and control feel.

entities.name: Stall Current vs ESC Rating and Duty-Cycle Thermal Limits
entities.summary: Explains how to size a drive ESC/driver's continuous and burst current ratings against a motor's stall current, and why sustained full-stall (e.g. pinned against a wall or opponent) is a thermal, time-limited event rather than something a small combat robot motor can hold indefinitely.
entities.expression: I_stall_total = n_motors * I_stall_per_motor;  esc_continuous_rating >= I_cruise_expected;  esc_burst_rating >= I_stall_total (with margin);  t_safe_stall is inversely related to I^2 (I^2*R resistive heating)

variables.I_stall_per_motor: stall current of one drive motor at the operating voltage, Amps
variables.n_motors: number of drive motors on that ESC/battery branch
variables.I_stall_total: worst-case simultaneous stall current draw, Amps
variables.I_cruise_expected: typical current draw while driving normally (well below stall), Amps
variables.esc_burst_rating: ESC/driver's short-burst peak current rating, Amps
variables.t_safe_stall: approximate time a motor can be safely held at stall before winding damage from resistive heating

entities.worked_example: Two FingerTech Silver Sparks, each 1.3A stall at 7.4V: I_stall_total = 2 x 1.3 = 2.6A combined worst case (both wheels pinned simultaneously). Normal cruising current is much lower, roughly 0.2-0.6A per motor. A drive ESC/driver should have a continuous rating comfortably above the cruising current (so it runs cool during normal driving) and a burst rating at or above the 1.3A per-channel stall figure with headroom (e.g. a 2-3A continuous per-channel rating is typical for antweight brushed ESCs). Because these small motors have very little thermal mass, holding full stall (e.g. wedged against an arena wall) for more than roughly 10-20 seconds risks overheating the winding insulation even though the ESC itself may tolerate the current — drivers are taught to 'bump' the throttle in short pulses rather than holding full stall continuously in a pushing match.

entities.name: Selecting a Gear Ratio from a Desired Top Speed
entities.summary: Rearranges the speed formula to solve for the gear ratio needed to hit a target top speed with a given motor and wheel diameter, then checks the result against the ratios actually available off the shelf.

variables.motor_rpm_no_load: no-load RPM of the bare motor at the chosen nominal voltage
variables.gear_ratio: gearbox reduction ratio needed, N:1 (solve for N)

entities.worked_example: Target: 8 mph top speed using a Silver Spark motor (motor_rpm_no_load = 11,530 at 7.4V) and a 2.0in wheel. gear_ratio = 11,530 x pi x 2.0 / (8 x 1056) = 72,444 / 8,448 ~= 8.6:1. Silver Spark's fastest stock ratio is 11.1:1, not 8.6:1, so an exact 8 mph target isn't reachable with this motor/wheel pairing off the shelf. Two fixes: (1) increase wheel diameter to 2.5in and re-check the stock 11.1:1 ratio: wheel RPM = 11,530/11.1 = 1,038.7, v_mph = 1,038.7 x pi x 2.5 / 1056 ~= 7.7 mph, very close to the 8 mph target; or (2) switch to a higher-RPM brushless drive pod (e.g. Repeat Robotics' 1106 gearmotor), which can exceed this speed range easily by running a higher supply voltage (3S/4S) instead of changing wheel size.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Mini Pro Brushed Antweight Gearmotor
entities.summary: Upgraded 16 mm brushed planetary antweight gearmotor with dual output bearings, a 4 mm hardened shaft, and four final-stage planet gears.
entities.notes: Dual ball bearings support the output shaft. Uses a custom-wound 030 brushed motor and 4x M2 face-mount holes on a 14 mm circle.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Tangent Drive 1406
entities.summary: Direct/tangent-drive 1406 brushless motor with the output shaft on the mounting side for compact antweight wheel drive.
entities.notes: Uses a 5 mm knurled tangent-drive shaft. Repeat suggests roughly 0.3-0.8 mm wheel interference depending on wheel material/design.

chunks.title: The 1 lb Antweight Drive Motor Landscape
chunks.body_md:
Antweight combat robots (1 lb / 454 g total weight) have a narrow but well-developed set of drive motor choices, almost all built around small brushed or brushless motors in the 12-16mm size range. The dominant, most trusted choice remains **FingerTech's Silver Spark**: a Mabuchi FK-050 brushed motor behind an all-metal 16mm spur gearbox, sold in nine stock ratios from a fast 11.1:1 to a crawling 600:1, all at the same ~29g weight and ~$19 price. Its budget sibling, the **Gold Spark**, uses the same base motor but a plastic final gear stage, trading some durability for a lower price (~$14.79) — fine for lighter-duty plastic antweights, riskier as the sole drive on a bot expected to take direct hits.

A newer and increasingly popular tier is **Repeat Robotics'** lineup: brushed and brushless planetary gearmotors that swap the Spark line's simple spur gearbox for a multi-stage all-metal planetary gearbox, which is generally more shock-tolerant and torque-dense for its size. Repeat's brushless "Mini" 1106 gearmotor (evolved through Mk3, Mk4, and Mk4.1 revisions) packages a custom-wound outrunner brushless motor directly into a 28.5:1 planetary gearbox with a hardened 4mm shaft, letting builders trade a simple brushed H-bridge for a reversing brushless ESC in exchange for higher efficiency and higher top speed at the same weight.

At the budget end of the market sit the generic **N-series gearmotors** (N10/N20/N30, 10-30mm motor cans) sold by dozens of overlapping AliExpress/Amazon/Banggood listings, often for a few dollars each in a huge range of ratios (30:1 up to 1000:1). These are the cheapest way to get a drive motor and are extremely popular in plastic antweights, but they carry a well-known "quality lottery" risk: two motors from the same listing, or even the same order, can have different windings, different gear materials (mixed metal/plastic despite "metal gear" branding), and different failure rates. **Pololu's micro metal gearmotors** (HP/MP/LP power tunes, many ratio options) sit between these tiers: a precision-manufactured 10x12mm metal gearbox with well-documented, consistent specs, at a price above generic N-series but usually below FingerTech/Repeat.

Finally, **modified or stock continuous-rotation 9g servos** offer the simplest possible drive for plastic antweights: no ESC required, direct receiver connection, at the cost of speed and torque. Choosing among these options is mostly a question of budget, desired reliability, and how much of the 454g weight budget is left after the weapon, battery, and armor.

chunks.title: FingerTech Silver Spark and Gold Spark: The Ratio Ladder Explained
chunks.body_md:
Both FingerTech Spark motors share the exact same base motor: a Mabuchi FK-050 brushed can rated for roughly 11,530 RPM no-load and 1.3A stall current at the 7.4V (2S LiPo) voltage most antweights run on, though FingerTech states it will run anywhere from 3V to 18.5V. What differs between Silver and Gold Spark — and between the ratios within each line — is entirely in the gearbox.

**Silver Spark** uses an all-metal spur gearhead across nine stock ratios: 11.1, 22.2, 33.3, 50, 83.3 (discontinued), 100, 200, 300, and 600:1. Weight climbs gently with ratio (28g at 11:1 up to 32g at 600:1) because the gearbox needs progressively more/larger gear stages to reach the higher reductions, but the motor and price stay constant across the whole family. The output shaft is a 3mm-diameter flatted shaft, standard length 38mm, with a shorter 22mm option on the 22:1/33:1/50:1 ratios for tighter builds — long enough that a wheel can be mounted directly onto it (a live-axle setup) without an intermediate shaft or bearing block, though FingerTech does offer an optional bearing block for extra support on the far side of the wheel.

**Gold Spark** uses the identical base motor but a gearbox with a plastic final gear stage, across a slightly different eight-ratio ladder: 20, 35, 50, 86, 115, 150, 250, and 360:1, all at a constant 28g and roughly 25% lower price than Silver Spark. FingerTech explicitly documents a mechanical ceiling on Gold Spark: output torque above 6.84 kg-cm (95 oz-in) will damage the plastic output gear stage, which caps how much of the higher-ratio end of the ladder (250:1, 360:1) can actually be exploited before self-destructing under stall.

Because no-load RPM and stall current are properties of the shared base motor, output RPM at any given ratio is simply 11,530 divided by that ratio, and output stall torque is (very roughly) the bare-motor stall torque (~0.046 kg-cm) multiplied by the ratio and by gearbox efficiency (~0.75 for Silver Spark's metal spur stages, somewhat lower for Gold Spark's plastic stage). This lets a builder pick a ratio directly from a target speed or torque without needing FingerTech's full published table for every combination. In practice, 22.2:1 through 50:1 covers most competitive antweight main-drive builds — fast enough to dodge and reposition, with enough torque margin over the traction limit to push confidently — while 100:1 and above are reserved for weapon lifters, self-righters, or bots that specifically prioritize crawling torque over speed.

chunks.title: Repeat Robotics: Brushed and Brushless Planetary Drive for Antweights
chunks.body_md:
Repeat Robotics built its antweight product line around one core idea: replace the simple spur gearbox found in motors like FingerTech's Spark line with a multi-stage, all-metal **planetary** gearbox, which generally handles shock loading and delivers torque more efficiently than a spur train of the same size. Their catalog spans both brushed and brushless motor options in the same 16mm-class form factor antweight builders are used to.

On the brushed side, the **Mini Brushed Mk2** (sold as the "Mini Pro Brushed" for around $25) offers a straightforward drop-in alternative to a Silver Spark, with the planetary gearbox as its main differentiator, at a modest price premium over FingerTech's spur-geared option.

On the brushless side, Repeat pioneered selling off-the-shelf 16mm brushless gearmotors specifically for combat robots — before this, brushless drive meant a builder sourcing a bare FPV-style outrunner motor and building or 3D-printing a custom gearbox around it. The **Mini Brushless** line went through several revisions: early Mk3/Mk4 versions used a custom-wound ~3500kv 1104-size motor; the current **Mk4.1** upgrades to a larger-stator 1106-size motor for more torque and power capability in the same envelope, paired with a 28.5:1 two-stage all-metal planetary gearbox and a hardened 4mm output shaft, weighing about 24g complete. Because it's brushless, it needs a reversing brushless ESC rather than a simple brushed H-bridge — Repeat sells a matching ESC designed specifically for their motors — but in exchange gets higher efficiency, no brush wear, and a rated 2S-4S voltage range that lets a builder retune top speed just by changing battery cell count rather than swapping hardware. A higher-spec "Mini Pro 1106" variant is also sold at roughly double the price for builders wanting the premium tier.

Repeat's catalog also includes larger motors like the Compact Brushless 1806 (marketed as the lightest brushless beetleweight drive motor on the market), useful context for how this same drive-pod architecture scales up a weight class, though it's oversized for a standard 1 lb budget. The general trade-off across Repeat's line versus FingerTech's Spark motors is: more durability and (for brushless) more speed/efficiency, at a real cost premium and, for brushless specifically, added ESC complexity and the sensorless-cogging caveats that come with any FPV-derived brushless motor run at very low speed.

chunks.title: N10/N20/N30 Gearmotors and the Quality-Lottery Problem
chunks.body_md:
The N-series family — N10 (smallest, ~10mm), N20 (most common, 12mm), and N30 (largest, ~30mm) micro gearmotors — is the budget backbone of plastic antweight and hobby-grade drivetrains. These motors are sold by dozens of overlapping resellers on AliExpress, Amazon, and similar marketplaces, almost always originating from the same small set of OEM factories, in an enormous range of stock gear ratios: 20:1, 30:1, 50:1, 75:1, 100:1, 150:1, 210:1, 250:1, 298:1, 380:1, and 1000:1 are all commonly available, alongside 3V/6V/12V motor voltage options.

The base N20 motor (before gearing) runs at roughly 15,000 RPM no-load at 6V — this is corroborated by real product listings, e.g. a 298:1 N20 gearmotor advertised and sold specifically as running 50 RPM at 6V (15,000 / 298 ≈ 50, a clean match). Gearbox length is constant across most ratios (~9mm) except 1000:1 (and sometimes 380:1), which get a 3.5mm-longer, reinforced housing rated for roughly 25 kg·mm (2.5 kg-cm) of continuous output torque versus ~20 kg·mm (2.0 kg-cm) for the standard ratios — a purely mechanical strength limit on the gear teeth, independent of how much torque the motor could theoretically produce electrically at that ratio.

The real problem with this whole family isn't the published spec sheet — it's that the spec sheet often doesn't reflect what actually arrives. Listings frequently advertise "metal gear" motors that turn out to have only some gear stages in metal and the rest in plastic, and even within a single order, individual units can vary in winding quality, no-load speed, stall current, and outright dead-on-arrival rate. This inconsistency is widely known in the antweight community as the "quality lottery." It doesn't make N-series motors unusable — plenty of successful plastic antweights run on them — but it does change how a builder should treat them: buy spares from the start and treat them as a semi-consumable part, bench-test every single unit before final installation (measuring free-run current and no-load RPM and rejecting any outlier compared to its batch-mates), and avoid depending on an untested cheap motor as the sole drive for an important match. Builders who want to skip this risk entirely pay the premium for FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, or Pololu motors instead, all of which publish (and generally meet) a consistent, verifiable spec.

chunks.title: Pololu Micro Metal Gearmotors: HP, MP, LP and Extended-Shaft Variants
chunks.body_md:
Pololu's micro metal gearmotor line sits in a useful middle ground between the quality-lottery risk of generic N-series motors and the higher price of FingerTech/Repeat combat-specific products: a precision-manufactured, well-documented 10x12mm all-metal gearbox on a 3mm D-shaped output shaft (9mm long), sold in a wide range of gear ratios and, distinctively, in three separate power tunes of the same base motor.

The three tunes — **LP** (Low Power), **MP** (Medium Power), and **HP** (High Power) — use the same physical gearbox and shaft but different motor winding/brush choices, trading current draw for speed and torque at any given ratio. At 6V, LP draws a stall current of about 0.36A (free-run ~40mA), MP about 0.67A (free-run ~70mA), and HP about 1.6A (free-run ~100mA). All three use shorter-life precious-metal brushes at 6V, which are lower-friction and preferred for these lower-current applications; Pololu also sells higher-voltage (12V) versions of some ratios with carbon brushes better suited to sustained higher-current use. For antweight drive, HP is the tune most builders reach for when they want the most power in the smallest package, while LP or MP make sense when a design is current-budget constrained, for example sharing a small ESC or battery branch with other electronics.

A useful variant is the **extended motor shaft** option, which brings the motor's rear shaft out through the back of the case in addition to the normal gearbox output shaft. This lets a builder mount a wheel-speed encoder disc, a second small pulley, or another accessory on the back of the motor without any machining — handy for a control-bot build that wants closed-loop wheel-speed feedback, or a 4WD layout that needs to drive an extra belt/pulley off the same motor.

The main trade-off versus FingerTech's Spark line is shaft length and mounting convention: Pololu's 9mm output shaft is too short for FingerTech's typical direct-wheel-mount (live-axle) approach and needs a hub or coupler, and Pololu doesn't publish a combat-specific mounting pattern the way FingerTech does. In exchange, a builder gets Pololu's much larger and more precisely documented range of ratios and power tunes, plus the reliability of a company whose entire business is measuring and publishing exactly this kind of spec — a meaningful advantage over generic N-series sourcing for a builder who wants predictable performance without over-paying for a combat-specific brand name.

chunks.title: Brushless Drive for Antweights: 1104/1106/1404 Motors, Pods, and Low-Speed Cogging
chunks.body_md:
Brushless drive on antweights has grown mainly out of the FPV micro-drone motor market. Motors labeled by a four-digit size code — **1104**, **1106**, **1404**, and similar — describe their stator dimensions (the first two digits are diameter in mm, the last two are stack height/length in mm): an '1104' is roughly 11mm in diameter and 4mm tall, an '1106' is the same 11mm diameter but a taller 6mm stack (more copper/stator volume, meaning more achievable torque and current handling at similar RPM), and a '1404' steps up to a 14mm diameter for still more capability in a similarly slim package. These motors are sold at a range of kv (RPM per volt) windings, and combat builders — or companies like Repeat Robotics who now sell them pre-integrated — pick a kv and pair it with a small gear reduction (commonly a 2-3 stage planetary gearbox in the 16-24mm class) to land in a useful antweight speed/torque range.

The major practical difference from brushed drive is that brushless motors require a **reversing brushless ESC** rather than a simple brushed H-bridge, and most of these motors are **sensorless** — they infer rotor position from back-EMF rather than dedicated Hall-effect sensors. Back-EMF is proportional to rotor speed, so at very low RPM (exactly the speed range a combat robot spends a lot of time in — creeping, jockeying for position, or making a fine positioning move) the signal an ESC needs to commutate smoothly gets weak and noisy. This shows up as **cogging**: jerky, notchy, sometimes stalling rotation right around zero speed, instead of the smooth linear response a brushed motor gives down to a full stop. **Sensored** brushless motors (with embedded Hall sensors) avoid this because the ESC always has a clean absolute rotor-position signal regardless of speed, but sensored micro combat motors are rarer and typically cost more; the more common combat-robotics fix is a gear reduction high enough that the motor itself is still spinning at a meaningfully high electrical RPM even when the wheel is barely turning, combined with an ESC/firmware tuned specifically for low-speed sensorless combat driving (as opposed to a generic multirotor ESC optimized for one direction and a fast spin-up) — which is exactly what purpose-built combat brushless ESCs like Repeat Robotics' reversing ESC are designed to handle.

The upside that keeps builders choosing brushless despite this complexity is power density and efficiency: no brushes to wear out, generally more torque and speed available per gram of motor than an equivalent brushed can, and (since kv and voltage set speed directly) the ability to retune top speed just by changing battery cell count (2S/3S/4S) rather than swapping hardware, useful for quickly adapting a drivetrain between a slower control-bot setup and a faster spinner-chassis setup.

chunks.title: Servo-Based Drive for Plastic Antweights
chunks.body_md:
Plastic antweights, built and raced on tight budgets and gram counts, have long used the cheapest, simplest drive mechanism available in the RC hobby world: the **9g micro servo**, modified (or purchased pre-modified) for continuous rotation. A normal hobby servo takes a PWM pulse (typically 1-2ms) and moves its output shaft to a corresponding angle, using an internal potentiometer to sense and hold position via a small feedback control loop. Removing that positional feedback — physically pulling the potentiometer and replacing it with two fixed resistors set to the servo's centered voltage, and usually clipping a mechanical stop tab inside the gearbox — breaks the position-holding behavior and turns the same PWM signal into a direct speed-and-direction command instead: a 1ms pulse spins one direction, 2ms spins the other, and roughly 1.5ms (the old 'centered' position) stops the motor. The result behaves almost exactly like a small ESC-driven gearmotor from the transmitter's point of view, but needs zero separate ESC or motor driver hardware — the servo plugs straight into a receiver channel.

Builders who don't want to do the modification themselves can buy factory continuous-rotation servos (commonly referred to by part numbers like FS90R) that ship ready to use, with more consistent centering than a hand-modified unit, at a small price premium over a basic positional 9g servo.

The appeal for plastic antweights is straightforward: at roughly 9g each, two servos plus a receiver is often the lightest and cheapest complete drive system available, with no ESC weight or cost, no separate motor-driver wiring, and a huge amount of freely available documentation and tutorials for the modification. The trade-offs are real, though. Servo gearboxes are built from a stack of small plastic gears sized for holding a load still, not for absorbing repeated combat impacts, and the motor inside is sized for positioning torque rather than continuous drive torque — so top speed and pushing power both fall well short of what a dedicated gearmotor-plus-ESC combination of similar weight can deliver. In practice, servo drive suits beginner builds, very light or defensive plastic antweights that don't need to win pushing matches, and builds where simplicity of wiring and zero extra electronics genuinely outweighs raw performance. Builders chasing a competitive edge in the plastic antweight class typically graduate to N-series or Pololu gearmotors with a small ESC once they're ready to trade some of that simplicity for speed and torque.

chunks.title: Wheels and Tires: Foam, Silicone, TPU, O-Rings, and Banebots
chunks.body_md:
Wheel choice on an antweight is a direct trade between weight, grip, shock absorption, and cost, and the options span a wide range of approaches.

**FingerTech Lite Flite foam wheels** are the default choice for most standard-material antweights: light neoprene foam tires available in diameters from 25.4mm to 76.2mm (1.0-3.0in) in 6.35mm (0.25in) steps, in two widths (12.7mm/0.5in and 19.1mm/0.75in), mounted via FingerTech's Lite, Snap, or Twist hub system. A 2.0in tire alone weighs only about 4g, and the foam's compliance absorbs shock from arena hazards and hard impacts that would otherwise transmit straight into the gearbox and shaft. Grip is described as "surprisingly good" for how light the material is, but it's still a step below purpose-built rubber compounds.

**Silicone-coated or cast-silicone tires** address that grip gap directly: a thin layer of 2-part silicone rubber, typically in the Shore A 30-50 durometer range, cast or brushed onto a foam or printed core. Softer compounds in that range grip best on polished wood or acrylic/polycarbonate arena floors, at the cost of faster wear and more debris pickup; it's a common DIY upgrade for control bots that need to win pushing matches rather than just drive around.

**3D-printed TPU wheels**, printed in flexible filament typically rated 85-95A Shore hardness, are the natural fit for plastic antweights: essentially free once a printer and filament are on hand, printable as a single piece with the hub bore built in (eliminating a separate hub's weight), and highly impact-resistant. Grip sits above rigid PLA/PETG wheels but below a soft cast-silicone tire at similar hardness.

**O-ring tires** are a cheap, DIY-friendly technique across weight classes: a plain hub (aluminum, printed, or Delrin) machined or printed with a groove sized for a rubber O-ring, stretched on as the tread. They're inexpensive to replace when worn, give solid rubber-compound grip, and let the hub itself stay very light — the main risk is the O-ring rolling in its groove under high torque if the groove isn't sized tightly enough.

**Banebots** wheels represent the name-brand compliant-tread option: the T61 line offers 6 hardness options (from a very soft, maximum-grip 10A yellow rubber up to a firmer, more durable 60A black rubber), 4 diameters, and 4 hub shaft sizes, while the smaller T40 line is aimed more specifically at ant/fairy-scale builds. Banebots wheels are heavier than foam or TPU for a given diameter — a real cost against a 1 lb weight budget — but their compliant tread conforms to the floor for grip and control that's hard to match with a rigid or foam alternative, which is why they show up more often on control-bot and pushing-focused designs than on speed- or weight-optimized spinners.

Across all of these, the general rule holds: softer/more compliant tread gives more grip but wears faster and adds weight/debris-pickup; harder/lighter tread (foam, rigid TPU) saves weight and lasts longer but gives up some pushing power to wheel slip on a smooth arena floor.

chunks.title: Drivetrain Topologies: 2WD, 4WD, Belt/Chain/Gear, Dead vs Live Axle
chunks.body_md:
The overwhelming majority of 1 lb antweights use **2WD direct (live-axle) drive**: two drive gearmotors, one per side, each with a wheel mounted straight onto its output shaft. This is the simplest, lightest, and most repairable layout — no belts, chains, or extra shafts to fail — and it's exactly what FingerTech's extra-long Silver Spark shaft is designed around. Its main limitation is that all of the robot's weight rides on two contact points (plus perhaps a rear skid or caster), so if one wheel is lifted off the ground (climbing over an opponent's wedge lip, or after a weapon hit), the robot can lose most of its drive traction at once.

**4WD** layouts address that by putting a powered wheel at each corner, giving redundancy (the robot still has drive even with one wheel airborne) and more overall traction for pushing matches, at the cost of extra weight and complexity. On a 1 lb budget, running four full motors is often too heavy, so 4WD antweights frequently use a **belt-driven** approach instead: one motor per side, with a small GT2 timing belt and pulley set (common because GT2 hardware is cheap and widely available from the 3D-printer supply chain) linking the front and rear wheel on that side so they spin together. This gets 4-wheel traction from only 2 motors, at the cost of belt tension/wear as an extra maintenance and failure point, and the belt run needs to be shielded from direct weapon hits. **Chain** drive is a heavier, more robust alternative to belts seen more often on larger weight classes, and **gear-driven** linkages (a small gear train connecting front and rear wheel shafts) are a third option that trades some efficiency for eliminating belt tension entirely.

A separate design axis is **dead axle vs live axle** mounting. In a live-axle setup (the antweight default), the wheel is mounted directly to the motor's output shaft, and that shaft is what takes the wheel's structural and impact loads. In a **dead axle** setup, the wheel spins freely on a fixed, non-rotating shaft (supported by its own bearings), and is driven separately — typically by a sprocket, pulley, or gear fixed to the wheel and linked back to the motor by a chain, belt, or gear train. This isolates the motor's own output shaft from direct impact loads (useful in wedge or lifter bots where a wheel might take a hard hit) and lets multiple wheels share a single structural axle, but adds parts, weight, and assembly complexity that most 1 lb antweights can't easily afford — dead axles show up far more often on beetleweight and larger designs.

Finally, **ground clearance and wheel guards** matter more on an antweight than the raw drivetrain numbers might suggest: exposed wheels are one of the most common ways to lose a match, since a stray hit from an opposing weapon (or even the arena floor's hazards) can destroy a wheel or knock a robot immobile in seconds. Competitive builds usually keep wheels tucked fully inside the body's footprint (inboard, not protruding past the armor line) and add minimal ground clearance — just enough to clear floor screws, seams, and hazards, no more — since every extra millimeter of clearance is extra exposed wheel and extra leverage for an opponent's wedge to get underneath.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Robot Speed from Motor RPM and Wheel Diameter
chunks.body_md:
The most basic drivetrain calculation a builder needs is converting a motor's rated speed into a robot's actual top speed on the floor. The relationship is: wheel RPM equals motor no-load RPM divided by the total gear ratio, and linear speed equals wheel RPM times the wheel's rolling circumference.

In a convenient mixed-units form: **v(mph) = (motor_rpm / gear_ratio) x pi x wheel_diameter(in) / 1056**. The constant 1056 converts inches-per-minute into miles-per-hour (there are 63,360 inches in a mile and 60 minutes in an hour, so 63,360/60 = 1,056).

**Worked example:** Take a FingerTech Silver Spark at its fastest stock ratio, 11.1:1, with a base motor no-load speed of 11,530 RPM (at 7.4V, the common 2S LiPo antweight voltage), paired with a 2.0in diameter wheel.

1. Wheel RPM = 11,530 / 11.1 = 1,038.7 RPM
2. v(mph) = 1,038.7 x 3.1416 x 2.0 / 1056
3. v(mph) = 1,038.7 x 6.283 / 1056 = 6,527 / 1056 ≈ 6.18 mph

This lines up well with commonly cited real-world antweight sprint speeds of roughly 6 mph across a short arena run. It's worth being clear about what this number is and isn't: it's a **theoretical no-load** top speed, calculated as if the motor were spinning completely unloaded at its rated voltage forever. In practice, actual top speed on the floor comes in lower — typically 70-90% of this figure — because of three effects this simple formula ignores: (1) **voltage sag**, since a small LiPo's internal resistance and the motor's own current draw pull the actual voltage at the motor below the pack's rated nominal voltage under load; (2) **rolling and gearbox friction losses**, which this formula doesn't subtract at all (it assumes 100% efficiency); and (3) the fact that a wheel does still need a small amount of torque even at 'cruising' speed to overcome friction, meaning the motor never quite reaches the true zero-load RPM the datasheet lists. Builders typically treat the no-load formula as a solid *upper bound* / rough comparison tool for choosing between ratios or wheel sizes, then confirm the real number with an actual timed run once the robot is built.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Sizing Motor Torque for a Target Acceleration
chunks.body_md:
Once a target top speed sets the gear ratio in the ballpark, the next question is whether that ratio can actually deliver the acceleration or pushing force the robot needs — this is a torque-sizing problem, not a speed problem.

Start from Newton's second law, F = m x a, to find the total force the robot needs at the ground. Convert that to a torque requirement at the wheel by multiplying by wheel radius and dividing across however many wheels share the load: **T_wheel = F x r / n_driven_wheels**. Finally, work back through the gearbox to the motor shaft itself: **T_motor_required = T_wheel / (gear_ratio x efficiency)**, using roughly 0.65-0.80 efficiency for a typical spur gearbox (like Silver Spark) or 0.80-0.92 for a planetary gearbox (like Repeat Robotics' motors).

**Worked example:** Take a standard 1 lb robot, m = 0.4536 kg, targeting an aggressive 2g acceleration (a = 19.6 m/s²) — a reasonable target for a bot that wants to close distance quickly or absorb a ram — on two driven wheels of 1.5in diameter (radius r = 0.019 m).

1. F = m x a = 0.4536 x 19.6 = 8.89 N
2. T_wheel (per side) = F x r / n = 8.89 x 0.019 / 2 = 0.0844 N·m ≈ 0.86 kg-cm
3. At a 33.3:1 gear ratio with ~0.75 gearbox efficiency: T_motor_required = 0.86 / (33.3 x 0.75) ≈ 0.0345 kg-cm

Compare that 0.0345 kg-cm requirement to the Silver Spark's bare-motor stall torque of roughly 0.046 kg-cm: there's real margin, meaning 33.3:1 comfortably supports a 2g start. Repeat the same math at the fastest stock ratio, 11.1:1: T_motor_required = 0.86 / (11.1 x 0.75) ≈ 0.103 kg-cm — more than double the bare motor's stall torque, meaning 11.1:1 alone cannot sustain a full 2g acceleration all the way from a dead stop under stall conditions (it can still accelerate, just not at that aggressive a rate, and the motor will spend less time near stall as RPM builds).

The practical takeaway: faster (lower) gear ratios trade away low-speed acceleration/pushing headroom for top speed, and slower (higher) ratios do the reverse. A builder picks the ratio that keeps enough torque margin for the robot's actual job (a control bot needs more low-end torque margin than a spinner that mostly just needs to reposition) — but as the next formula shows, that torque margin only matters up to the point where the wheels can actually put it to the ground.

chunks.title: Worked Example: The Traction Limit and Why Extra Torque Gets Wasted
chunks.body_md:
No matter how much torque a drivetrain can theoretically produce, it can only push as hard as the wheels' grip on the floor allows before they simply spin in place. That ceiling is the **traction limit**: F_max = μ x N, where μ is the coefficient of friction between the wheel tread and the arena floor, and N is the normal force (weight) pressing the driven wheels down.

**Worked example:** A 1 lb robot weighs 0.4536 kg x 9.81 m/s² = 4.45 N. Fit it with silicone-tread wheels giving a friction coefficient around μ = 0.6 against a typical polycarbonate arena floor (foam alone would be lower, roughly 0.3-0.5; a soft compliant tread can push toward 0.7-0.8). F_max = 0.6 x 4.45 = 2.67 N — that's the absolute maximum forward force this robot can generate on this floor, no matter what drivetrain sits behind the wheels.

Now compare that to what the drivetrain itself can supply. Take the lowest-torque stock Silver Spark ratio, 11.1:1, with an estimated output stall torque around 0.38 kg-cm (≈0.0373 N·m) per motor, on the same 1.5in-diameter (0.019m radius) wheels, split across 2 driven wheels: the wheels together can theoretically deliver up to F = 2 x T / r = 2 x 0.0373 / 0.019 ≈ 3.9 N of force before the *motors* stall out. That's already above the 2.67 N traction ceiling — meaning this robot's wheels will slip and spin before its motors ever reach their torque limit, even at the fastest, lowest-torque ratio in the whole Silver Spark lineup.

This is the core reason "just gear it down more for more pushing power" is often a wasted move on a well-traction-matched antweight: once a drivetrain's available torque already exceeds the traction limit, adding more torque (by choosing a higher, slower gear ratio) doesn't increase real-world pushing force at all — the extra torque just goes into wheel slip, heat, and battery drain, while the robot gets slower and less maneuverable for no pushing benefit. The useful design target, as commonly recommended in the antweight community, is to size the drivetrain with roughly 1.5-2x the torque strictly required to reach the traction limit (giving margin for wear, voltage sag, and imperfect weight distribution) and then spend any additional gear-ratio choice on speed and control feel rather than further torque, since torque beyond that point is traction-limited, not motor-limited.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Stall Current, ESC Ratings, and Duty-Cycle Heating
chunks.body_md:
Every drive motor draws its highest current right at stall (zero RPM, full voltage applied) — this is the number an ESC, wiring, connectors, and battery all need to be sized to survive, at least briefly, even though the robot won't spend most of a match sitting at true stall.

**Worked example:** A 2WD antweight running two FingerTech Silver Sparks, each rated 1.3A stall current at 7.4V. Worst case, both motors stall simultaneously (e.g. the robot is pinned against a wall while still commanding full throttle): I_stall_total = 2 x 1.3A = 2.6A combined. Normal cruising current while driving freely is much lower, typically in the 0.2-0.6A-per-motor range, since a motor only draws current in proportion to the torque it's actually producing, not its theoretical maximum.

Sizing rule of thumb: an ESC or motor driver's **continuous current rating** should sit comfortably above the expected cruising current (so it runs cool through normal driving), while its **burst/peak current rating** needs to clear the full per-channel stall current with some safety margin — for a 1.3A-stall motor, a driver rated for 2-3A continuous per channel is typically adequate, which is why most small antweight brushed ESCs (FingerTech's own boards among them) are specified in that range.

The part that trips up new builders is the **duty-cycle / thermal** side of this, separate from the ESC's rating entirely: these tiny motors have very little thermal mass, so even a stall current well within the ESC's rated capability can still cook the motor's own windings if held for too long, because resistive (I²R) heating in the coil accumulates faster than the small motor can shed it. As a rough guide, holding a Silver Spark-class motor at full stall for more than about 10-20 seconds starts to risk winding insulation damage, even though the ESC itself may show no signs of distress. This is why experienced drivers are taught to **"bump" the throttle** — short pulses of full stall rather than holding it — during a pushing match or when momentarily jammed against an obstacle, treating the stall current rating as a brief-duration limit rather than something the motor can sustain indefinitely.

chunks.title: Worked Example: Reverse-Solving Gear Ratio from a Target Top Speed
chunks.body_md:
When a builder starts from a target top speed instead of a specific motor, the speed formula can be rearranged to solve directly for the gear ratio needed: **gear_ratio = motor_rpm_no_load x pi x wheel_diameter(in) / (target_mph x 1056)**.

**Worked example:** Suppose the goal is an 8 mph top speed, using a FingerTech Silver Spark (motor_rpm_no_load = 11,530 at 7.4V) and a 2.0in wheel.

gear_ratio = 11,530 x 3.1416 x 2.0 / (8 x 1056) = 72,444 / 8,448 ≈ **8.6:1**

But Silver Spark's fastest stock ratio is 11.1:1, not 8.6:1 — there's no off-the-shelf ratio fast enough to hit exactly 8 mph with this motor and this wheel size. This is a completely normal outcome of the reverse calculation, and it points to two practical fixes:

1. **Increase the wheel diameter** and re-check the fastest available stock ratio. At 11.1:1 with a larger 2.5in wheel: wheel RPM = 11,530 / 11.1 = 1,038.7, so v(mph) = 1,038.7 x 3.1416 x 2.5 / 1056 ≈ **7.7 mph** — very close to the 8 mph target, achieved with a completely off-the-shelf Silver Spark by simply choosing a bigger wheel instead of hunting for a nonexistent ratio.
2. **Switch to a higher-RPM drivetrain entirely**, most commonly a brushless drive pod. Because a brushless motor's speed is set by kv x voltage rather than a fixed brush-motor RPM, a brushless antweight gearmotor can be tuned well past this target simply by running a higher-cell-count battery (3S or 4S instead of 2S), without touching the gearbox or wheel at all.

The general lesson from reverse-solving gear ratio this way is that **wheel diameter and gear ratio are interchangeable knobs for hitting a speed target** — a builder isn't locked into whatever stock ratios a motor happens to ship in, because changing wheel size (within the traction and torque limits from the other formulas) shifts the achievable speed just as effectively as changing the gearbox. The final choice usually comes down to whichever knob has the least negative side effect on the rest of the build: a bigger wheel raises ground clearance and can increase rotational inertia (slower spin-up/braking) and often adds weight, while a different gear ratio may not exist as a stock part, and a different motor altogether means a bigger BOM and design change.

chunks.title: Recommended Drivetrain: Competitive 1 lb Antweight Spinner
chunks.body_md:
A competitive antweight spinner spends most of its weight budget on the weapon system (motor, bar/disc, containment) and armor, so the drivetrain's job is to be light, reliable, and "just fast/agile enough" to line up hits and dodge — not to win pushing matches. Recommended baseline:

- **Topology:** 2WD direct (live-axle) drive. A spinner rarely needs 4WD's extra traction, and every gram saved on the drivetrain can go into the weapon or armor instead.
- **Motors:** A pair of FingerTech Silver Spark gearmotors in the 22.2:1-33.3:1 range are the proven default — enough torque margin over the traction limit for confident repositioning, with a reasonable top speed (roughly 4-6 mph depending on wheel size) for closing distance and dodging counter-attacks. Builders chasing extra speed and efficiency at similar weight increasingly use a Repeat Robotics brushless "Mini" 1106 drive pod instead, which can be tuned faster on 3S while staying in the same weight class as a Silver Spark pair.
- **Wheels:** 1.25-1.5in FingerTech Lite Flite foam wheels, prioritizing shock absorption (protecting the drivetrain from the vibration and impacts of being near an active spinning weapon and from opposing hits) over maximum grip — a spinner's own gyroscopic effects and hit-and-retreat playstyle rely less on sustained high-friction pushing than a control bot does.
- **Ground clearance and wheel guards:** Keep wheels tucked fully inside the body's outer footprint, ideally behind a hardened skirt or armor lip, since exposed wheels are one of the most common ways a spinner robot gets killed — a single solid hit to an unguarded wheel can end the match instantly.
- **Battery/voltage:** 2S LiPo (7.4V) is the standard baseline; 3S is worth considering specifically to unlock a brushless drive pod's higher speed range, but adds weight that must be budgeted against the (typically much heavier) weapon system.

The overarching principle for a spinner's drivetrain is: size it to comfortably clear the traction limit with margin (per the traction-limit formula) at a ratio that gives useful positioning speed, then stop — any drivetrain weight or complexity beyond that is weight the weapon system could have used instead.

chunks.title: Recommended Drivetrain: 1 lb Antweight Control Bot
chunks.body_md:
A control bot (wedge, rammer, or full-body pusher) lives or dies by its ability to win sustained pushing exchanges, hold a heading under load, and stay mobile after taking a hit — so its drivetrain deserves a noticeably larger share of the weight budget than a spinner's. Recommended baseline:

- **Topology:** 4WD is genuinely worth its weight cost here, more so than on any other antweight archetype, because losing traction on even one corner during a pushing match can mean losing the match outright. The common, weight-efficient way to get there on a 1 lb budget is 2 motors per side linked front-to-rear with a small GT2 belt and pulley set, rather than 4 full independent motors.
